name: Crowdsourced verified-compatibility databases
what_it_is: A class of public, opt-in, crowdsourced databases where end users submit measured hardware/software results that are then aggregated and made browsable so others can look up 'will X run on my Y' before committing. Classic precedents span gaming (System Requirements Lab's 'Can You Run It', which matches a user's detected hardware fingerprint against a requirements database and gives a yes/no gate plus the component that caused the answer) and benchmarking (OpenBenchmarking.org, which offers optional/opt-in uploading of benchmark result data with anonymous statistics reporting). The pattern has recently appeared in the local-LLM space: llm.aidatatools.com is an Ollama-based local-LLM benchmark whose results are automatically submitted to a community database, letting users compare throughput across Apple Silicon, NVIDIA GPUs, and various CPU configurations.
real_precedent: System Requirements Lab 'Can You RUN It' (https://www.systemrequirementslab.com/cyri); OpenBenchmarking.org opt-in result uploads (https://openbenchmarking.org/test/pts/ollama); llm.aidatatools.com — Ollama local-LLM benchmark that auto-submits to a community database (https://llm.aidatatools.com/). These are directly analogous crowdsourced-result databases; the aidatatools one is the closest local-model/Ollama precedent.
evidence_of_impact: 'Can You Run It' is a long-running, heavily-used compatibility gate and requirements database that scans hardware and matches setups (https://www.systemrequirementslab.com/cyri). OpenBenchmarking.org sustains a public corpus specifically because uploading is opt-in and anonymous-statistics-based, showing the opt-in model can accumulate real data (https://openbenchmarking.org/test/pts/ollama). The aidatatools Ollama benchmark demonstrates the exact 'submit-your-local-LLM-result-to-a-shared-DB' pattern already exists and attracts contributions across Apple Silicon/NVIDIA/CPU (https://llm.aidatatools.com/); Ollama itself is cited at ~52M monthly downloads, indicating a large potential contributor base. [uncertain] Exact submission counts, unique contributors, and adoption figures for these databases were not independently verified (source pages returned 403 to automated fetch; figures come from search-result summaries).
applicability_to_agentdyno: AgentDyno's 'dyno doctor' already produces exactly the structured triple these databases are built from: model + hardware + agent-target with a graded pass/fail on tool-call probes (P1-P3). 'dyno scan' already captures the hardware fingerprint (GPU/VRAM/CPU/RAM), and 'connect' ties results to a concrete agent target (Goose/Cline), giving a rare third axis (agent compatibility) that no existing DB has. A concrete build: add an opt-in 'dyno doctor --share' flag that POSTs an anonymized record (hardware fingerprint, quantized model+backend llama-server/Ollama, agent target, probe grades) through the existing local gateway to a hosted public DB, then expose a lookup ('dyno fit' could query 'has anyone verified Qwen3-8B Q4 + Cline on a 3060?'). The differentiator vs llmfit-style calculators is that entries are real, run-verified doctor exams, not modeled estimates — 'verified model+hardware+agent combos, submitted by real users' is a genuine, buildable moat.
build_effort: medium — the CLI already emits structured doctor/scan results, so the client-side capture is nearly free. Real cost is: (1) an explicit opt-in consent + anonymization flow (hardware fingerprints and model choices are PII-adjacent), (2) a hosted backend + database + dedup/normalization, (3) a public browse/query UI or CLI query path, and (4) light moderation/verification to keep submissions trustworthy. None individually is large, but it moves AgentDyno from a pure local tool to also operating a hosted service.
risk_or_caveat: Cold-start: a compatibility DB is worthless until it has coverage, and local-LLM combinatorics (model x quant x backend x hardware x agent) are huge, so sparse data can look empty for most queries. Privacy/consent is a real hazard — the project's own guidelines flag a data-egress consent gap, so silent or default-on sharing would backfire. Submissions are hard to truly 'verify' (users can spoof or misreport), so 'verified' must mean cryptographic/attested doctor runs or it becomes UserBenchmark-style disputable data. Running a hosted DB adds ongoing cost, moderation, and an attack surface that a local Apache-2.0 tool otherwise avoids.
